what: US Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship in blow to Trump

clean_source_blocks.text: Watch: Supreme Court's birthright ruling is major blow to Trump, says BBC's Gary O'Donoghue The Supreme Court has ruled that babies born in the US have a constitutional right to citizenship, rejecting Donald Trump's bid to end the 150-year-old policy. In a 6-3 decision, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled that children born in the US "to parents unlawfully or temporarily present" are "citizens at birth" under the 14th amendment. President Trump had sought to limit the right through an executive order, arguing that the children of undocumented immigrants and some temporary visitors were not "subject to the jurisdiction thereof", and thus not eligible for birthright citizenship. The ruling is a major setback for Trump's immigration agenda, and has been welcomed by civil rights groups. Watch: Americans react to Supreme Court upholding birthright citizenship
The ruling is a major setback for Donald Trump's immigration agenda, and has been welcomed by civil rights groups.

Trump called the ruling “too bad for our Country”, but said the US Congress should now take up the matter legislatively, suggesting another avenue to keep the issue alive. “No long and unwieldy Constitutional Amendment is necessary! Congress should start TODAY to work on ending expensive and unfair to our Country, Birthright Citizenship,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “They will have my Complete and Total Support!” Civil rights groups and Democrats celebrated the ruling from the conservative court, calling it one of the most important decisions in the modern era and noting how it affirmed the promise of the United States.

Court rules against Trump administration on policy that people born in the United States are citizens The US supreme court has upheld the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, affirming that nearly all people born on US soil are American citizens and rejecting a central pillar of Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda. The president had issued an executive order on the first day of his second term that sought to deny automatic citizenship to the children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents. Writing for the majority, Chief Justice John Roberts said this order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution.

In a 6-3 decision, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled that children born in the US "to parents unlawfully or temporarily present"  are "citizens at birth" under the  14th amendment.

President Trump had sought to limit the right through an executive order, arguing that the children of undocumented immigrants and some temporary visitors were not "subject to the jurisdiction thereof", and thus not eligible for birthright citizenship.

The ruling is a major setback for Trump's immigration agenda, and has been welcomed by civil rights groups.

"No long and unwieldy constitutional amendment is necessary," he said. "Congress should today start work on ending expensive, and unfair to our country, birthright citizenship."

Court rules against Trump administration on policy that people born in the United States are citizens

The US supreme court has upheld the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, affirming that nearly all people born on US soil are American citizens and rejecting a central pillar of Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda.

The president had issued an executive order on the first day of his second term that sought to deny automatic citizenship to the children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents. Writing for the majority, Chief Justice John Roberts said this order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution.

“Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights – to freely participate in our political community,” wrote Roberts. “The Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to ‘every free-born person in this land.’ We keep that promise today.”

Roberts was joined by the liberal justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, and the conservative justice Amy Coney Barrett. The conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred with the judgment but dissented in part, arguing that the executive order violated federal law but not the constitution. The court’s writings in the ruling span 194 pages, nearly 90 of which were written by Thomas in dissent, his longest in his tenure on the court.

payload.title: Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus piti syntymäpaikkaan perustuvan kansalaisuuden voimassa
payload.summary: Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus on hylännyt Donald Trumpin yrityksen rajoittaa syntymäpaikkaan perustuvaa kansalaisuutta. Ratkaisu vahvistaa, että Yhdysvalloissa syntyneillä lapsilla on perustuslaillinen oikeus kansalaisuuteen myös silloin, kun heidän vanhempansa ovat maassa ilman lupaa tai tilapäisesti.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus on ratkaissut, että Yhdysvalloissa syntyneillä lapsilla on perustuslaillinen oikeus maan kansalaisuuteen, ja torjunut presidentti Donald Trumpin pyrkimyksen lopettaa noin 150 vuotta voimassa ollut käytäntö. Päätös on merkittävä takaisku Trumpin maahanmuuttopolitiikalle ja vahvistaa syntymäpaikkaan perustuvan kansalaisuuden asemaa Yhdysvalloissa.

## Päätös nojasi 14. lisäykseen

Korkein oikeus päätyi ratkaisuun äänin 6–3. Enemmistön kannan kirjoittanut päätuomari John Roberts totesi, että Yhdysvalloissa syntyneet lapset ovat syntyessään kansalaisia 14. perustuslain lisäyksen perusteella myös silloin, kun heidän vanhempansa ovat maassa laittomasti tai tilapäisesti.

Trump oli pyrkinyt rajaamaan oikeutta presidentin määräyksellä. Hänen hallintonsa argumentti oli, että paperittomien maahanmuuttajien ja joidenkin tilapäisesti maassa olevien ulkomaalaisten lapset eivät kuuluisi perustuslain muotoilun mukaisesti Yhdysvaltojen tuomiovallan piiriin, eikä heille siksi syntyisi automaattista kansalaisuutta.

Oikeus katsoi kuitenkin, että määräys rikkoi Yhdysvaltain perustuslain 14. lisäystä. Ratkaisu vahvistaa tulkinnan, jonka mukaan lähes kaikki Yhdysvaltain maaperällä syntyneet ihmiset ovat Yhdysvaltain kansalaisia. Päätös koskee keskeistä osaa Trumpin maahanmuuttoagendasta, sillä määräyksellä olisi pyritty kieltämään automaattinen kansalaisuus paperittomien maahanmuuttajien ja tilapäisten ulkomaalaisten asukkaiden lapsilta.

## Trump haluaa viedä asian kongressiin

Trump arvosteli päätöstä ja kuvasi sitä maalleen huonoksi. Hän sanoi, että Yhdysvaltain kongressin pitäisi nyt tarttua asiaan lainsäädännön kautta, mikä viittaa siihen, että hän pyrkii pitämään kysymyksen poliittisella asialistalla oikeuden ratkaisusta huolimatta.

Trump kirjoitti Truth Social -palvelussaan, ettei pitkää ja raskasta perustuslain muutosta hänen mukaansa tarvita. Hän kehotti kongressia aloittamaan työn syntymäpaikkaan perustuvan kansalaisuuden lopettamiseksi ja lupasi hankkeelle täyden tukensa.

## Kansalaisoikeusjärjestöt juhlivat ratkaisua

Kansalaisoikeusjärjestöt ja demokraatit ottivat ratkaisun vastaan myönteisesti. Heidän mukaansa konservatiivisen korkeimman oikeuden päätös vahvistaa yhden Yhdysvaltojen perustuslaillisen lupauksen ja kuuluu nykyajan merkittävimpiin oikeusratkaisuihin. Ratkaisu jättää voimaan periaatteen, jonka mukaan Yhdysvalloissa syntyminen tuo kansalaisuuden perustuslain nojalla.
summary_bullets: Yhdysvaltain korkein oikeus vahvisti syntymäpaikkaan perustuvan kansalaisuuden perustuslaillisen suojan.
Päätös torjui Donald Trumpin määräyksen, jolla oikeutta olisi rajattu paperittomien ja tilapäisesti maassa olevien ulkomaalaisten lapsilta.
Trump arvosteli ratkaisua ja kehotti kongressia jatkamaan asian käsittelyä lainsäädännön kautta.

Watch: Supreme Court's birthright ruling is major blow to Trump, says BBC's Gary O'Donoghue The Supreme Court has ruled that babies born in the US have a constitutional right to citizenship, rejecting Donald Trump's bid to end the 150-year-old policy. In a 6-3 decision, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled that children born in the US "to parents unlawfully or temporarily present" are "citizens at birth" under the 14th amendment. President Trump had sought to limit the right through an executive order, arguing that the children of undocumented immigrants and some temporary visitors were not "subject to the jurisdiction thereof", and thus not eligible for birthright citizenship. The ruling is a major setback for Trump's immigration agenda, and has been welcomed by civil rights groups. Watch: Americans react to Supreme Court upholding birthright citizenship

The ruling is a major setback for Donald Trump's immigration agenda, and has been welcomed by civil rights groups.

Trump called the ruling “too bad for our Country”, but said the US Congress should now take up the matter legislatively, suggesting another avenue to keep the issue alive. “No long and unwieldy Constitutional Amendment is necessary! Congress should start TODAY to work on ending expensive and unfair to our Country, Birthright Citizenship,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “They will have my Complete and Total Support!” Civil rights groups and Democrats celebrated the ruling from the conservative court, calling it one of the most important decisions in the modern era and noting how it affirmed the promise of the United States.

Court rules against Trump administration on policy that people born in the United States are citizens The US supreme court has upheld the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, affirming that nearly all people born on US soil are American citizens and rejecting a central pillar of Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda. The president had issued an executive order on the first day of his second term that sought to deny automatic citizenship to the children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents. Writing for the majority, Chief Justice John Roberts said this order violated the 14th amendment of the US constitution.
